x.A: An internet gateway with a default route makes the subnet public. The instance would also need a public IP address, and it would be exposed to the internet, which the design avoids.
x.B: A NAT gateway in a public subnet, with the private subnet's default route pointing to it, gives the instance outbound-only internet access to download updates. Inbound connections from the internet are not allowed.
x.C: A NAT instance must sit in a public subnet to reach the internet gateway. Placing it in the private subnet means it has no internet path.
x.D: This has the same problem as C, since the NAT instance is in the private subnet, and routing the default route straight to the internet gateway turns the subnet public.

x.A: EFS is a shared file system that many EC2 instances can mount at once. It grows automatically and stores data redundantly across multiple AZs.
x.B: An EBS volume attaches to a single instance in one AZ (apart from Multi-Attach in special cases), so it isn't simultaneously accessible from multiple servers and its redundancy is limited.
x.C: Glacier Deep Archive is long-term archive storage with slow retrieval, so it isn't accessible simultaneously from application servers.
x.D: AWS Backup is a backup service and not a storage system the application servers can read and write to.

x.A: Policy 1 gives only iam:Get* and iam:List* actions, which are read-only, so the engineer can't delete IAM users.
x.B: Policy 1 allows ds:*, which would include deleting directories, but Policy 2 explicitly denies ds:Delete*. An explicit deny overrides an allow, so deleting directories is blocked.
x.C: Policy 1 allows ec2:* on all resources, which includes terminating (deleting) instances, and nothing denies it. The engineer can delete EC2 instances.
x.D: Policy 1 gives only logs:Get* and logs:Describe*, which are read actions, so the engineer can't delete CloudWatch logs.

x.A: Security group rules can't use an instance ID as a source or destination.
x.B: A rule that references the security group ID of another tier allows traffic only from instances in that group. It follows least privilege and stays correct as instances are added or replaced.
x.C: The VPC CIDR block allows every resource in the VPC, which is far broader than needed between tiers.
x.D: A subnet CIDR block allows every instance in the subnet, which is broader than the tier's security group and is harder to keep accurate.

x.A: Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations like S3 and isn't a queue the payment service reads from, and it doesn't prevent duplicate orders.
x.B: A CloudTrail rule triggered by logged requests is not a dependable workflow, and it can fire more than once for resubmitted forms.
x.C: SNS pushes messages to subscribers and can't be polled by the payment service, and it doesn't guarantee exactly-once handling.
x.D: The order is stored once, and its number is sent to an SQS FIFO queue, which provides exactly-once processing and ordering. The payment service processes it and deletes the message, so a resubmitted form doesn't create duplicate orders.

x.A: A read-only ACL would stop users from modifying and uploading documents, which the requirements allow.
x.B: Versioning keeps every version of a document, so modifications and deletions don't overwrite earlier versions, and all versions stay available.
x.C: An IAM policy attached to the bucket doesn't prevent accidental deletion, and policies attach to identities, not to buckets.
x.D: MFA Delete requires an MFA code to permanently delete versions, which prevents accidental deletion.
x.E: KMS encryption protects data at rest but doesn't prevent accidental deletion or keep versions.

x.A: A CloudWatch metric stream sends Auto Scaling metric data in near real time to Firehose, which writes to S3. It is serverless and runs outside the instance launch path, so launches aren't slowed.
x.B: An EMR cluster is not serverless and is far more infrastructure than the need calls for.
x.C: A scheduled Lambda function isn't near real time and would have to poll for status, so data would be delayed.
x.D: A bootstrap script that installs the Kinesis Agent runs during instance launch, which slows launches, and it wouldn't capture Auto Scaling events across the account.

x.A: A Lambda function must download and convert 1 GB files, which can exceed Lambda's memory, temp storage, or 15 minute limit, and handling Parquet conversion needs custom code.
x.B: A Spark job triggered by Lambda needs a cluster or runtime to run it, so it adds operational overhead.
x.C: Using Athena queries from a scheduled Lambda to convert isn't triggered by each upload, and it takes more steps than a Glue job.
x.D: A Glue ETL job converts CSV to Parquet in a serverless way and scales for 1 GB files. A Lambda function triggered by each S3 PUT event starts the job, so there is no infrastructure to manage.

x.A: AWS Backup creates consistent, restorable daily backups of RDS and keeps them in a vault for the chosen period. A backup plan with a daily schedule and a 2 year expiry meets the retention requirement with little effort.
x.B: RDS retains automated backups for at most 35 days, and Data Lifecycle Manager manages EBS snapshots, not RDS snapshots, so this doesn't work.
x.C: Transaction logs in CloudWatch Logs are not consistent, restorable backups of a database.
x.D: DMS CDC to S3 captures changes but is not a consistent, restorable backup, and it needs a replication instance to run.

x.A: An AD Connector is a directory proxy for AWS applications and isn't how FSx for Windows File Server uses Active Directory, and IAM groups can't control SMB file and folder permissions.
x.B: Tags don't control SMB access, and IAM groups aren't used for file and folder permissions.
x.C: A service-linked role gives FSx permissions to AWS resources, not file-level access control for users.
x.D: Joining the FSx file system to the self-managed Active Directory lets the existing AD groups and NTFS permissions control access to the shares, folders, and files after the move.

x.A: CloudFront can cache different versions of content based on request headers such as device type, so customers on different devices get the right version from the edge.
x.B: A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4 and can't route based on host headers.
x.C: A Lambda@Edge function can inspect the User-Agent header and send the matching version of the content for each device.
x.D: An NLB doesn't support host-based routing, because that is an ALB feature, and Global Accelerator doesn't solve device-specific content.
x.E: An NLB doesn't support path-based routing either, and it doesn't see the device type.

x.A: VPC peering is the lowest-cost way to connect the two VPCs. Adding routes on both sides and allowing the application's security group in the ElastiCache cluster's inbound rule gives access.
x.B: A transit VPC needs extra EC2 instances and management, so it costs more than peering.
x.C: Peering connections don't have security groups. The rule has to be on the ElastiCache cluster's security group.
x.D: A transit VPC is more expensive and complex, and it doesn't have a security group that controls this access.

x.A: An ECS cluster provides container orchestration that AWS manages, so there is no orchestration software to run yourself.
x.B: Running the Kubernetes control plane on EC2 means managing the infrastructure, which the company can't do.
x.C: The EC2 launch type still needs you to manage and scale the EC2 instances that host the containers.
x.D: The Fargate launch type runs the tasks without servers to manage, and two or more tasks give availability and scaling with little maintenance.
x.E: Managing your own Kubernetes worker nodes on EC2 is extra infrastructure to maintain.

x.A: Simple routing with health checks can't return only healthy records, since simple routing records don't support health checks.
x.B: A failover policy is for a primary and a secondary, not for 10 instances that should all serve traffic.
x.C: CloudFront with EC2 as an origin doesn't do health checks of individual instances this way, and it isn't designed to fix DNS returning unhealthy IP addresses.
x.D: An ALB with health checks sends traffic only to healthy instances, and Route 53 routes to the ALB, so DNS always returns a healthy endpoint.

x.A: Public EC2 instances are exposed to the internet directly, which is less secure.
x.B: CloudFront can't use EC2 instances in private subnets as an origin, since they aren't reachable from CloudFront directly.
x.C: The EC2 instances are in private subnets, so only the public ALB is exposed, and CloudFront serves HTTPS content from the edge using the ALB as the origin. This is the most secure design.
x.D: Public instances are less secure, and using the instances as the origin instead of the ALB loses load balancing.

x.A: Global Accelerator uses the AWS global network to send users to the closest healthy ALB endpoint, and it continuously monitors endpoint health and redirects traffic quickly. It gives low and consistent latency.
x.B: CloudFront with Lambda functions caches content but isn't suited to latency-sensitive game traffic that isn't cacheable.
x.C: An S3 origin doesn't fit a game application that runs on EC2 behind ALBs.
x.D: DynamoDB with DAX speeds up data reads but does not monitor application health or redirect traffic across Regions.

x.A: A Kinesis data stream doesn't store data in S3 by itself, and invoking Lambda to feed Kinesis Data Analytics adds custom components.
x.B: A data stream doesn't deliver to S3 by itself, and an EMR cluster is a lot of operations for near-real-time analysis.
x.C: Firehose can convert to Parquet and encrypt, but EMR is a cluster to manage, so it costs more effort for the analytics.
x.D: Firehose ingests the data, encrypts it, converts it to Parquet, and stores it in S3. Kinesis Data Analytics analyzes it in near real time. Both are fully managed.

x.A: ElastiCache in front of the database caches frequent reads, such as scores, so most reads no longer hit the database. It takes small application changes and fixes the read performance.
x.B: RDS Proxy pools connections and helps with connection spikes but doesn't reduce read load on the database.
x.C: Moving to Lambda is a big architecture change and doesn't address database read performance.
x.D: Migrating to DynamoDB is a major change to the data model and the application.

x.A: Exporting to DynamoDB would need a different data model and query approach, so analysts can't just run their SQL queries.
x.B: ElastiCache is a cache for key-value lookups and doesn't run SQL queries for analysts.
x.C: A read replica gives analysts a separate copy to query with SQL, so the primary database is no longer slowed down, and the web application doesn't change.
x.D: Redshift would work for analytics but needs a data pipeline and more setup, so it is more than minimal changes.

x.A: Client-side encryption encrypts the data before it is uploaded, so it is encrypted at rest before it reaches S3, and using HTTPS covers encryption in transit.
x.B: Server-side encryption happens after S3 receives the data, so it doesn't encrypt the data before upload.
x.C: A bucket policy that requires SSE-S3 enforces server-side encryption after the upload begins, not before the data leaves the client.
x.D: Default bucket encryption with KMS is also server-side and happens after the data reaches S3.

x.A: A higher minimum capacity keeps extra instances running all day, which costs more than needed.
x.B: A higher maximum capacity only raises the ceiling and doesn't make the group scale up faster.
x.C: Scheduled scaling can raise capacity to the needed level shortly before 1 AM, so the group is ready when the jobs start, and it can scale back down after.
x.D: Adding more instances per scaling step still reacts after load arrives, so it won't have full capacity at the start.

x.A: Replacing the dynamic website with a static S3 site isn't possible because the site is dynamic.
x.B: CloudFront with the ALB as the origin caches content at edge locations worldwide, so it serves users quickly without rebuilding the architecture in more Regions. Caching on Accept-Language returns the right language version.
x.C: API Gateway caching in one Region doesn't bring content close to users around the world.
x.D: Launching EC2 instances with NGINX in each Region means building and managing infrastructure in many Regions, which the company doesn't want.

x.A: A pilot light deployment keeps only core infrastructure running and must be scaled up on failover, so its recovery time is longer than a warm standby.
x.B: An Aurora global database replicates to the DR Region with typically under a second of lag, and a warm standby runs a scaled-down copy of the whole environment that can scale up quickly. This gives the lowest RTO.
x.C: RDS Multi-AZ stays within one Region, so it doesn't replicate to the DR Region, and pilot light is slower to recover.
x.D: RDS Multi-AZ doesn't provide a cross-Region copy of the database, so the DR Region's database wouldn't be up to date.

x.A: Using Lambda and custom scripts to deploy infrastructure is more work to build and maintain than a CloudFormation template.
x.B: Copying AMIs to another Region costs little during normal operation, and CloudFormation can automate building the infrastructure there within the 4 hour RTO. It is a backup-and-restore strategy that uses the fewest resources.
x.C: Keeping EC2 instances running all the time in a second Region uses more resources than needed for a 4 hour RTO.
x.D: A second AZ doesn't protect against a Region failure, and running instances all the time uses more resources.

x.A: A scheduled action sets the desired capacity to 20 shortly before the office opens, so the instances are ready at the start of the day. It still scales down afterwards, so cost stays low.
x.B: Step scaling at a lower CPU threshold still reacts after the load arrives, so staff may still see slowness at the start.
x.C: Target tracking at a lower threshold is reactive too, and a shorter cooldown doesn't have capacity ready before users arrive.
x.D: Setting both the minimum and maximum to 20 keeps the group fixed at 20 and removes the ability to scale down, which costs more.
